# Abstract

Hayman's approach analyses a complete diallel (parents, $F_1$ and reciprocals) for gene action: an analysis of
variance that separates additive, dominance, maternal and reciprocal effects; the variances $V_r$ and covariances
$W_r$ of the arrays and their graph; the components $D$, $H_1$, $H_2$, $F$, $h^2$ and $E$; and tests of the
additive-dominance model.

# The analysis

```{r hayman}
h <-
  Hayman(
      y      = Yield
    , Rep    = Rep
    , Cross1 = Cross1
    , Cross2 = Cross2
    , data   = HaymanData
    )
knitr::kable(x = h$ANOVA, digits = 3)
```

Line $b_1$ tests the mean dominance deviation of the crosses from the parents (directional dominance), $b_2$ whether
this deviation differs among parents, $b_3$ the remaining dominance. Maternal and reciprocal effects are not
significant here.

# Arrays: $V_r$ and $W_r$

After averaging reciprocal crosses, array $r$ (the progeny of parent $r$) has variance $V_r$ and covariance $W_r$
with the parents:

```{r arrays}
knitr::kable(x = h$Wr.Vr.Table[, c("Wr", "Vr", "Wr.Minus.Vr", "Wr.Plus.Vr", "Yr")], digits = 2)
```

# The $W_r$-$V_r$ graph

```{r graph, fig.height = 5}
plot(h)
```

Under the additive-dominance model the points lie on a line of unit slope (dashed) inside the limiting parabola
$W_r^2 = V_r V_{0L0}$. Parents near the origin carry mostly dominant genes, parents far from it mostly recessive
genes.

# Tests of the model

```{r tests}
knitr::kable(x = h$Tests, digits = 4)
```

A significant $t^2$ or a slope that differs from 1 indicates epistasis or correlated gene distribution; the
components below then need care. In this data set the slope is negative and differs from 1, so the
additive-dominance model is not adequate.

# Components of variation

```{r components}
knitr::kable(x = h$Components.of.Variation, digits = 3)
knitr::kable(x = h$Other.Parameters, digits = 3)
```

$\sqrt{H_1/D}$ above 1 indicates overdominance; $H_2/(4H_1)$ below 0.25 an unequal distribution of positive and
negative alleles among the parents.

# Summary

Hayman's analysis asks how genes act rather than which parents combine well; read the components only when the
tests support the additive-dominance model.

# References

Hayman, B. I. (1954). The theory and analysis of diallel crosses. *Genetics*, 39(6), 789--809.

Hayman, B. I. (1954). The analysis of variance of diallel tables. *Biometrics*, 10(2), 235--244.

Mather, K. and Jinks, J. L. (1982). *Biometrical Genetics*, 3rd edition. Chapman and Hall, London.

Singh, R. K. and Chaudhary, B. D. (2004). *Biometrical Methods in Quantitative Genetic Analysis*. Kalyani Publishers,
New Delhi.
